summary: This informational document provides principles for the operation of Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) registries. It was replaced by RFC 8720.

eli5.summary: IANA keeps lists of numbers and names that protocols use. This sets out the guiding ideas for running those lists fairly. It was replaced by RFC 8720.

questions: how should iana registries be operated
subtitle: Seven principles for running the global registries that Internet protocols depend on.

tldr.problem: Internet protocols depend on centrally managed registries of identifiers and constants. Without clear principles for how these registries operate, people and systems cannot trust the values they find there.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7500 establishes seven core principles: identifiers must be unique, stable, and predictable; registries must be public, open, and transparent; and registry operations must be accountable to the community that uses them.
tldr.outcome: These principles provide a foundation for trust in IANA registries, ensuring that protocol identifiers have consistent meanings across all implementations. It was replaced by RFC 8720.

facts.label: Core principles
facts.value: Seven: uniqueness, stability, predictability, public, open, transparent, accountable

today: RFC 7500 was obsoleted by RFC 8720, which provides updated principles for IANA registry operation. The underlying principles of uniqueness, stability, transparency, and accountability continue to guide registry management.

sections.title: Introduction: Why Registries Matter
sections.content:
The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) maintains registries of protocol identifiers: constants, port numbers, type codes, and other values that Internet protocols use to communicate. At the time RFC 7500 was written, IANA maintained over two thousand protocol parameter registries. Almost every Internet protocol uses registries in some form.

Historically, RFC publication and IANA registry management were handled by the same person (Jon Postel of USC), but today they are operated by separate entities. Internet registries hold the authoritative record of identifier meanings, so trust in these registries is essential to the trust in the protocols themselves.
sections.eli5: The Internet uses thousands of lists of standard numbers and codes. For example, port 80 means HTTP. Someone has to keep these lists accurate and fair, or the whole Internet gets confused.

sections.title: The Seven Core Principles
sections.content:
RFC 7500 establishes seven principles for registry operation. Uniqueness ensures the same identifier is never used for two different purposes. Stability requires that identifier assignments last; they should not be reassigned except after careful consideration. Predictability means the assignment process must not include unexpected steps, though it need not have a fixed deadline when expert judgment is involved.

Public registries are made freely available to everyone in well-known locations. Open and Transparent processes allow all interested parties to participate and observe policy decisions. Accountable registries answer to the communities that rely on them through mechanisms such as contracts, service level agreements, and oversight bodies.
sections.eli5: The principles are: use each number only once, keep assignments permanent, make the process predictable, publish the lists freely, let anyone watch how decisions are made, and answer to the people who use them.

sections.title: Uniqueness, Stability, and Predictability
sections.content:
Protocol developers rely on identifiers having consistent meanings across all implementations. Uniqueness guarantees that if two parties use identifier 6 in the same protocol, they mean the same thing. Stability means an organization can depend on an identifier's meaning not changing without warning. Developers build code that uses identifier 6 for TCP, and that meaning must not change.

An identifier can only be reassigned after careful consideration of the impact and, if possible, with consent of the original assignee. Predictability does not require a fixed timeline; processes involving expert review may take longer. Rather, it means no unexpected steps are introduced: the process is open and parties can understand what happens at each stage.
sections.eli5: Each code means exactly one thing, forever. If port 80 means HTTP today, it means HTTP tomorrow. Processes are clear so people know what to expect.

sections.title: Public, Open, and Transparent Operations
sections.content:
Public registries are made freely available without restrictions in locations that change infrequently and only after adequate notice. Open processes allow all interested parties to participate in setting registry policy and making assignments. Transparent operations mean registry policy decisions and expert recommendations are visible to the public and subject to challenge or appeal.

When a registry is established, a policy is set for adding new entries and updating existing ones. If the policy becomes unclear in practice, the registry operator should provide feedback to allow improvement. Importantly, when registry operators are not involved in establishing policy, this avoids the perception of favoritism or unfairness.
sections.eli5: The lists are posted online for free. Anyone can suggest a new code. Decisions about what gets added are made in public, not in secret.

sections.title: Accountability Mechanisms
sections.content:
Registry operations must be accountable to the affected community. For protocol parameters, the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) has oversight responsibility, and the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC) maintains a service level agreement with the registry operator (currently ICANN). Both bodies are accountable to the Internet community through the IETF Nominating Committee process.

For Internet number registries (IP addresses and domain names), oversight is performed by Regional Internet Registries (RIRs). RIRs are member-based organizations accountable through elected governance boards. Policy development is coordinated by a community-elected number council and subject to process review before ICANN Board approval.
sections.eli5: The IAB and other oversight bodies check that the registry operator is doing a good job and serving the community fairly. The oversight bodies answer to the Internet community through elections.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: RFC 7500 is an informational document providing guiding principles for IANA registry operation. It was made obsolete by RFC 8720, which provides an updated set of principles. The core ideas of uniqueness, stability, public access, and community accountability remain central to how IANA registries operate.
sections.eli5: This document was replaced by RFC 8720, which provides updated principles while the registries themselves continue to operate the same way.
